text: 1 Belgrade 1961; 2 Cairo 1964; 3 Lusaka 1970; 4 Algiers 1973; 5 Colombo 1976; 6 Havana 1979; 7 New Delhi 1983 (India hosted); 8 Harare 1986; 9 Belgrade 1989; 10 Jakarta 1992; 11 Cartagena 1995; 12 Durban 1998; 13 Kuala Lumpur 2003; 14 Havana 2006; 15 Sharm el-Sheikh (Egypt) 2009; 16 Tehran 2012; 17 Margarita 2016; 18 Baku 2019; 19 Kampala 2024 (latest).
APMIP (since 2003): AP ranks 1st in micro-irrigation; Rayalaseema 64% of area; AP has converged MGNREGA with the AP Micro Irrigation Project.
Lucknow Metro (Sept 2017) was the latest metro to open at the time of the 2017 exam (after Kochi, June 2017); Kanpur, Agra, Bhopal, Indore and others opened later.
AP outlay ₹10,134 crore (2026-27); as of 1 Apr 2026, 42 projects; network 100% electrified; 74 Amrit Bharat stations (Sullurupeta opened 22 May 2025).
"Original NPP target" = 2045; "current / revised target" = 2070. TFR 2.1 was reached only around NFHS-5 (2019-21).
Nearly 70% of elderly women lack a formal pension vs about 40% of elderly men; ageing could cut GDP growth by about 70 basis points a year (IMF).
CAG performance audit of IAY: found under-assessment of the housing shortage (not over-assessment), non-transparent beneficiary selection and low-quality houses.
Per capita income grows faster at current prices than at constant prices because the constant-price series allows for the rise in the price level (UPSC 2000).
India (UPSC 2015): GDP at market prices in rupees has risen steadily; real GDP growth has fluctuated (e.g. contraction in 2020-21) → "Only II".
Base year: 2022-23 in the new series released 27 Feb 2026 (earlier 2011-12); it uses double deflation and Supply-Use Tables. GDP at current prices 2024-25 = Rs 318.07 lakh crore (new series).
Nominal growth exceeds real growth by roughly the inflation rate; 2025-26 estimates (old series): nominal 8.0%, real 7.4%.
Growth = rise in real output: a growing country has rising GNP at constant prices (APRO 2008); GDP growth data is the usual yardstick (Polytechnic Lect. 2020).
GDP deflator = nominal GDP ÷ real GDP × 100 = ratio of GDP at current prices to constant prices (G2 Mains 2025) – not real ÷ nominal.
First Plan (1951-56): achieved growth 3.6% against a 2.1% target – the figure APPSC 2019 keys as "GDP growth 1950-51" (strictly it is the First Plan average, not a single-year rate).
IAS 2010: GDP did not rise four-fold in 2000-10 (about three-fold at current prices); the public sector's share of GDP declined after liberalisation.
Number questions: answer the first official estimate current at the exam date; real vs nominal is the usual trap (2016-17: 7.1 real, 11.0 nominal).
At current prices PCI rises faster than at constant prices (constant prices remove inflation).
Per capita NNI 2025-26 (FAE, Jan 2026, current prices): ₹2,47,487, up ₹16,025; the 2026 new series lowered nominal GDP and PCI.
2016-17: per capita NNI ₹1,03,219 (+9.7%); 2017-18: PCI at current prices up about 8.6% (CSO provisional).
2006-07 (UPSC 2008): per capita GDP at current prices about ₹37,000; wheat about 75 mt; rice about 93 mt (not 180) → A and C.

Older per capita income figures (current prices): 1991-92 about Rs 7,500 (keyed); 2010-11 Rs 54,527 (Advance Estimate, Feb 2011) → Rs 53,331 (Quick Estimate, Jan 2012; 2009-10 Rs 46,117), at 2004-05 prices Rs 35,993; 2013-14 Rs 74,380; 2018-19 Rs 1,26,699 (Economic Survey 2018-19).
Miracle economies: GDP growth of 7% for a decade or more (NextGen) – not 8, 8.5 or 7.5%.
Real income = current income × 100 / price index; e.g. Rs 30,000 crore × 100 / 150 = Rs 20,000 crore.
Gross domestic saving 2000-01: 23.4% of GDP at current market prices (Economic Survey 2001-02).

2011-12 series criticism: manufacturing growth not matching physical indicators; private corporate sector overestimated via MCA-21. Arvind Subramanian (former CEA, 2019): select indicators and GDP growth "flipped" post-2011; 2011-17 growth about 4.5%, not ~7%.
2024-25, current prices: primary 21.4%, secondary 25.8%, tertiary 52.9% – figures to quote now; the new series shows higher agriculture and industry shares, lower services.
Mining and quarrying ≈ 3% of GVA in 2016-17 at 2011-12 prices (about 2.4% at current prices) – small output share, key raw-material supplier.
NSS uses three reference periods (year, week, day); "Usual / Current Monthly Status" is NOT an NSSO approach.

Jobless growth: a widening gap between GDP growth and employment growth – more goods and services produced without proportionate jobs; NCERT dates the "disheartening development" to the late 1990s; employment growth was near zero again in 2004-05 to 2009-10 (the decade 2001-2010 in the AEE 2016 key).
Best / most appropriate measure of growth: growth of per capita real income year to year – not national income at current prices (inflation, population), not GDP/NDP/NNP totals.
HDR 2025 recalculated India's 2022 value as 0.676 (rank 133). Inequality cuts India's HDI by 30.7%. No newer HDR had been released as of Nov 2026.
Both the Lakdawala and Tendulkar groups were poverty-estimation committees; a question asking "which one" usually wants the latest offered (Tendulkar).
Latest: monthly PLFS (CWS) rate 5.5% in May 2026 (5.2% April); 30-35 million seasonal labourers migrate every year (7 Sep 2026).
new: Latest: monthly PLFS (CWS) rate **4.9%** in **October 2026** (5.0% September); 30-35 million seasonal labourers migrate every year (7 Sep 2026).
why: MoSPI's October 2026 monthly PLFS bulletin puts unemployment at 4.9% (Sept 5.0%); May 2026 is no longer the latest

text: 1. A plan for the current year (with the annual budget).
Sixth Plan targets: GDP growth 5.2%; exports to grow about 10% a year (APPSC key).
Eighth Plan State Plans: States' own contribution at 1993-94 prices (-) 4% (negative balance from current revenues).
Second Plan: planned public outlay Rs 4,800 crore (private Rs 3,100 crore); actual Rs 4,600 crore (Rs 3,650 crore investment + Rs 950 crore current).

Twelfth Plan financing (public sector): largest source = borrowings incl. net miscellaneous capital receipts (Rs 36.99 lakh crore of Rs 80.50 lakh crore), then balance from current revenues (Rs 23.47 lakh crore), then PSE resources (Rs 20.03 lakh crore).
'Decade of jobless growth': the 1990s (1991-2000) – organised employment lagged far behind GDP growth.
RBI Governor in 1991: S. Venkitaramanan (Dec 1990 – Dec 1992); then C. Rangarajan (1992-97). Manmohan Singh (Governor 1982-85) was Finance Minister.
How many so far: 16 (as of 2026); in 2014 the count was 14.
Vijay Kelkar was earlier Union Finance Secretary (1998-99); he also led the tax-reform task forces – not CAG or Planning Commission head.
16th FC: annual CAG-certified disclosure of net tax proceeds.
Raising SLR locks more funds in liquid assets (kept by the bank itself; CRR is kept with RBI) → fewer loanable funds; an SLR cut frees funds.
CRR increase → banks have less to lend.
CRR cut 100 bps to 3.0% of NDTL → about ₹2.5 lakh crore released – announced 6 June 2025, in four 25-bp tranches (fortnights from 6 Sep, 4 Oct, 1 Nov, 29 Nov 2025), fully in force by Dec 2025.
Asked ×9 (APPSC JL, FRO 2022). Trap: the APPSC FRO 2022 limit was ₹10 lakh; CGPSC 2024 "at present" = ₹20 lakh.
AP ranks 1st in SHG-bank linkage: about 36% national share, 99.66% recovery.
Data localisation (RBI, April 2018): entire payment-system data must be stored only in India – no public-sector ownership or CAG audit condition → "Only I".

Monetary (and credit) policy is formulated and implemented by the RBI (MPC since 2016; six members) – the RBI regulates and announces the repo and reverse repo rates, not the Finance Ministry, PM, President, CAG or SBI.

RBI controls "money and credit" and controls credit creation by commercial banks through quantitative (Bank Rate, repo, CRR, SLR, OMO) and qualitative (selective credit control, margins, moral suasion) tools.
A-R (APPSC 2024): institutions ensure stability through monetary policy because central banks use repo and CRR to manage liquidity and inflation – R explains A.
Raja J. Chelliah was never an RBI Governor (tax-reform economist); Usha Thorat was a Deputy Governor.
CRR = Cash Reserve Ratio: the share of a bank's Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that it must keep as cash balances with the RBI (CDS 2020; APPSC AEE 2008).
"Required reserve ratio" = the certain percentage of deposits every bank must keep as reserves = CRR (APPSC Degree Lecturers 2023).
CRR is fixed by the RBI (the central bank), not the Finance Ministry or the market (APPSC G2 2011); governed by Section 42 of the RBI Act, 1934; no floor or ceiling since 2006.
Banks get no interest on CRR balances; CRR is in cash only.

Raising CRR: commercial banks have less money to lend (not the RBI or the Union Government) → liquidity falls, credit creation falls → helps control inflation (UPSC 2010 ×4; UPPSC 2004, 2010; CGPSC 2017).
APPSC: a CRR hike causes fall in money circulation and low demand for goods and services (I and II); it does NOT raise purchasing power or the banks' lending capacity.

Lowering CRR: credit creation increases (APPSC G2 2017); banks get higher leverage to liquidity and the economy may see increased investment (NextGen: lower CRR "helps banks provide loans … for investment purposes" and "boosts the growth rate").

Temporary I-CRR (Aug 2023): 10% on the increase in NDTL (19 May–28 Jul 2023), announced 10 Aug 2023, effective fortnight from 12 Aug; impounded about ₹1.1 lakh crore; released in phases (9 Sep, 23 Sep, 7 Oct 2023) (APPSC G2 Mains 2025: both statements correct).
CRR applies to the whole NDTL; the I-CRR applied only to the incremental deposit base (not to "new borrowers") (APPSC 2024).

SLR: minimum share of NDTL a bank keeps with itself in liquid assets before lending – cash, gold and unencumbered approved/Government securities (G-secs, T-bills, SDLs); not priority-sector loans (APPSC 2023: I, II and III).
SLR = mechanism by which commercial banks provide credit to the Government (they buy G-secs to meet it) (UPSC 2010 ×3).
Older wording "ratio between cash in hand and total assets" = SLR (UPSC 1998; UPPSC 2007) – strictly SLR is liquid assets to NDTL.
Governed by Section 24, Banking Regulation Act, 1949; range 0%–40% of NDTL; the 25% floor was removed by the BR (Amendment) Act, 2007; MSS securities count towards SLR.
SLR cut of 50 bps → more lendable funds → scheduled commercial banks may cut lending rates (UPSC 2015 ×2) – not "GDP up drastically" or "liquidity down".
Raise SLR to fight inflation; cut SLR for growth.
Trap: SLR "19.25%" (APPSC G2, 2019 review) is now 18%; "required reserve ratio" = CRR, not SLR.
9 Feb 2013: CRR cut 25 bps to 4% (Third Quarter Review, Jan 2013).

Rate at which RBI lends short-term to banks / at which banks borrow from RBI = Repo rate (UPPSC 2005, 2008, 2013; SI 2019; APPSC G2; AP recruitment); comes under monetary policy; used to regulate liquidity (APPSC G2 2017).
Rate at which banks lend to / park funds with RBI = Reverse repo (UPPSC 2008 ×2).
LAF (June 2000): the window through which banks borrow via repos and lend via reverse repos – "borrowing through repurchase agreements" = LAF (APPSC G2).
Repo − reverse repo gap: 1.00 percentage point in June 2010 – June 2011 (from Sep 2010); from May 2011 only repo is fixed and reverse repo set 100 bps below it.
Corridor width 50 bps: SDF = repo − 25 bps; MSF = Bank Rate = repo + 25 bps. Fixed-rate reverse repo 3.35% (May 2026), used at RBI's discretion since SDF.
Selective controls of RBI: margin requirements and moral suasion – not CRR/SLR (CDS 2017).
Inflation rising steadily → central bank increases the repo rate (SSC 2020).
Anti-inflation set: raise Bank Rate, CRR and SLR – buying G-secs is expansionary (UPPSC RO 2016: 1, 2 and 3).
Expansionist policy would NOT increase the MSF rate; it would cut SLR, Bank Rate and repo (UPSC 2020: only II).
CRR/SLR cut → more lendable funds and a higher money multiplier; policy rates regulate the capacity for credit creation.
Monetary policy = macro policy on money supply, framed by the RBI (APPSC Welfare Organiser; UPPSC 2006) under the RBI Act, 1934; the MPC fixes the repo rate since 2016.

APPSC 2024 statements: CRR hike reduces credit creation (I ✗); I-CRR targeted incremental deposits, not borrowers (II ✗); tenor premium is an MCLR component (III ✓); MSF is an overnight rate equal to Bank Rate, not long-term or lower (IV ✗) → only III.
Dated questions are keyed to the date asked; "current" rates change at each MPC meeting (next: 2-4 Dec 2026).
6 members (3 RBI + 3 external) – not 12, not reconstituted every year, chaired by the RBI Governor, not the Finance Minister (UPSC 2017: only I).
After the 2019-20 mergers there are 12 public sector banks (SBI + 11 nationalised banks) (as of 2026).
C. D. Deshmukh: first Indian RBI Governor; Finance Minister 1950-56.
75% = SFB PSL share = RRB PSL share = payments bank share of demand deposits in SLR securities.

What N-I asked to cut: SLR (38.5% → 25%), CRR (15% → 3-5%) and priority-sector (directed) credit (to 10%) – so "SLR, CRR and priority sector financing" (NextGen), not just "SLR and CRR". N-I did not set the 10% CRAR (that was N-II).
Exam angle: N-I = Financial System (1991); N-II = Banking Sector Reforms (1998). Recommendation questions test SLR/CRR/PSL cuts (N-I) vs 3 tiers and 10% CRAR (N-II).

Reforms covered banking, capital, government debt and forex markets: CRR and SLR cuts (SLR 38.5% in 1991-92), deregulation of interest rates, entry of private firms in banking and insurance, prudential norms on NPAs, end of selective credit controls – "all of the above" in such MCQs.

Shadow banking = credit creation by financial institutions outside the regular banking regulatory framework (hedge funds, NBFCs; also unregulated activities of regulated entities) – they escape CRR/SLR and capital rules.
Inflation rate = year-on-year % change in CPI (current month's CPI over the CPI of the same month last year).
A fall in the inflation rate means only that prices are rising more slowly – not that prices fell, food supply rose or industry stagnated.
Repo rate (as of 7 Oct 2026): 5.50% (was 5.25% in Aug 2026); repo acts on demand, cannot directly fix supply shocks (onion, crude oil).
Laspeyres index: base-year (initial-year) quantities as weights; Paasche: current-year weights; Fisher's ideal index = geometric mean of the two.
Household savings reach government via bank deposits (SLR holdings), small savings/NSSF, insurance and PF.
Early-1990s double-digit inflation was controlled by containing the budgetary deficit and unproductive expenditure.
GFD (financing side) = net borrowing at home + borrowing from RBI + borrowing from abroad (RAS 2023). Net borrowing at home includes small savings and, indirectly, bank SLR holdings.
RD, FD, PD were adopted as official terms from 1997-98 (Ramesh Singh); budget deficit stopped being the headline measure after ad hoc T-bills ended (1997).
Interest rate, CRR, bank rate, credit ceiling = monetary tools, NOT fiscal (APPSC FSO; RAS 2023).
Since the 2018 FRBM debt definition, the debt statement also values external debt at current exchange rates.
Best way to finance a current account deficit = FDI; twin deficit = FD + CAD (dissaving cuts national savings).
Objectives: inter-generational equity, long-run macro stability, eliminate RD, cut FD, debt management, transparency. Fixing the repo rate is NOT an FRBM objective.
After bifurcation AP could not meet its FRBM targets: CAG put AP's 2014-15 FD at ₹31,717 crore = 6.10% of GSDP (2 June 2014-31 March 2015 accounts), double the 3% ceiling.
States' revenue receipts: own tax revenue is the largest component (~50%, FY25); share in Central taxes second (~32%); CAG average 2014-24: own tax 47%, tax share 28%, grants 17%.
Short-term asset: held up to 24 months (general rule); LTCG 12.5% (as of Aug 2026); indexation uses the Cost Inflation Index (CBDT, base 2001-02).
Not an advantage: GST does not "drastically cut the current account deficit" or make India "overtake China" (UPSC 2017: only I).
Current (revenue) account income: corporation tax, profits of public enterprises, excise duties; NSC sales and World Bank loans are capital (UPPCS 1998).
CAG is not involved in preparing the Budget – it audits the accounts after the money is spent (its reports go to the PAC); the Finance Commission award and ministries' estimates feed the Budget.

Charged expenditure (Art. 112(3)): discussable, not voted – President's emoluments, presiding officers' salaries, SC judges' salaries and pensions, HC judges' pensions only, CAG, UPSC, debt charges, court decrees.
Public Accounts Committee = Parliament's control over the audit of the Budget (examines CAG reports); approves excess grants first.
Data questions: answer for the year the question names; the explanation then gives the current figure.
India's trade on current account (goods + services) is largest with the USA.

UPSC 2020 (present): merchandise exports < imports; services exports > services imports; India runs an overall trade/current account deficit → 1, 3 and 4 (imports of iron & steel, fertilisers, machinery did NOT fall).
BoP has two main accounts – the current account and the capital account (NextGen); it is not "only capital" or "only current" or "only exports and imports".
IMF BPM6 uses three accounts – current, capital and financial; the RBI generally combines capital and financial under "Capital Account".
Among CRR, SLR, demonetisation and forex reserves, only foreign currency reserves relate to the BoP – its overall balance shows up as a change in reserves.
Current account = goods + services + income + transfers; it includes the Balance of Trade. Capital receipts and payments are NOT part of it (CDS 2014).
Capital account (UPSC 2013): foreign loans, FDI and portfolio investment – private remittances are current account (so codes with remittances are wrong). FDI is NOT current account.
Current-account balance = exports − imports of goods and services + net primary income + net secondary income.
Gift to foreigners = debit in the current account; gift from foreigners = credit; exports of goods/services = credit.
Current + Capital + Financial account + Net Errors & Omissions = 0 – BoP always balances in accounting terms; a surplus in one account = deficit in another. BoT need not balance.
The rupee is fully convertible only on the current account – not on the capital account (still partial) and not into gold (UPSC 2000).
IMF Article VIII makes current account convertibility obligatory; India accepted it in August 1994 (operationalised 19 Aug 1994).
UPSC 2001 A-R: current-account forex ceilings were changed in 2000 under FEMA, but foreign currency assets did not fall (rose from $38.0 bn, March 1999 to $42.3 bn, March 2001) – R false.
A country with a large current-account surplus has a larger capacity to give aid and loans abroad.
PPP theory: equality of purchasing power (the inflation differential) decides the long-run rate of exchange. Long-run anchors (ES 2025-26): PPP, savings-investment balance, current account.
India: full current account convertibility (Aug 1994), only partial capital account convertibility.
India's current policy: market-determined exchange rate (managed float).
Andhra Pradesh: rank 12th in FDI inflows (2019-20 PYQ); FDI $608.59 mn in FY 2025-26 (from $92.13 mn in 2023-24, $233.14 mn in 2024-25); metallurgical industries led.
Operational holding: all land used for farm production and operated as one technical unit by one person, alone or with others, regardless of title, size or location.

1 Forests; 2 Area under non-agricultural uses; 3 Barren and unculturable land; 4 Permanent pastures and grazing land; 5 Land under miscellaneous tree crops; 6 Culturable waste land; 7 Current fallows; 8 Fallows other than current fallows; 9 Net sown area. Net irrigated area is NOT a category.
Kharif 2026 (El Niño): AP rainfall 51% below normal (1 June-25 Aug); sown 20.35 vs 25.63 lakh ha; shift to pulses and drought-resilient crops (as of 2026).
Dated-figure PYQs use the estimate current at the exam: 209.8 MT printed for 2001-02 was really the 1999-2000 output; 1983-84 output is "130-150 MT".
Interval: the 2015 scheme said a card once in every 3 years (AEE 2016 key); in practice cards are now issued free every two years (cycles 2015-17, 2017-19).
ATMA in AP: all 26 districts, 60:40 funding; disseminates latest technologies and fills adoption gaps through bottom-up planning (SREP).
AIDIS (NSS 70th round, debt as on 30 June 2012): average debt of a rural household ₹32,522 (urban ₹84,625) – nearest option ₹25,000.
Stree Nidhi recovery rate: 94.4% of loans (as on 31-10-2016).
Small Farmer Large Field (UPSC 2023): many marginal farmers in an area organise into groups and synchronise/harmonise selected operations – they work as one large field (no land surrender).
Buffer norms fixed by CCEA quarterly – as on 1 April, 1 July, 1 October, 1 January; 1 April norm 210.40 LMT (rice 135.80, wheat 74.60).
Most-asked angle (about 14 PYQs): the year 1991 and the licensing count. APPSC's "at present" answer is 4 (DPIIT 2019); "18" is the July 1991 figure.
Methods: cross-holding, warehousing, minority sale, OFS, IPO/FPO, CPSE ETF, Bharat 22, buyback, strategic sale – methods of disinvestment (SLR, CRR, repo are NOT).
HDI 2019 (HDR Dec 2019): Norway 1st; India's HDI 2022 (HDR 2021/22) rank 132nd.
AP: services = AP's largest sector – about 43% of GVA (current prices) (APPSC DL 2020).
Livestock = largest contributor to GVA at current prices in the 2021-22 AE too (ahead of fishing, manufacturing, horticulture); about ₹1.5 lakh cr = 30.87% of agri GVA (2023-24).

Exam angle: match the year to the trio – 2016-17 AE 31.77 : 22.23 : 46; 2021-22 36.19 : 23.36 : 40.45; 2024-25 35.29 : 23.18 : 41.53. "Largest sector" = services; "largest sub-sector at current prices" = livestock.
Compiled by the Directorate of Economics & Statistics (DES), AP (not NSO) at current and constant 2011-12 prices; 3 sectors, 17 sub-sectors (agriculture 5, industry 4 incl. construction, services 8).
AP grew slower than India in 2023-24 and faster from 2024-25; in 2025-26 faster on both current and constant prices.
Current-price record: 17.36% (2021-22) in the earlier SRE (15.64% TRE).
Undivided AP, 2010-11 (advance estimate): GSDP ₹5,67,636 crore at current prices, 19.44% over 2009-10.
1999-2006: AP's primary sector ranked 2nd among States by compound growth rate.
India's PCI (older series): per capita NNI at current prices ₹74,380 (2013-14); ₹35,993 (2010-11, 2004-05 prices); about ₹6,835 (≈ ₹7,500) in 1991-92; it grew 8.6% from 2016-17 to 2017-18.
Best district in GDDP (current prices), 2017-18 (13 old districts): East Godavari (Krishna close behind).
Visakhapatnam ranked 1st in PCI (FY 2025-26); drivers: Vizag Port, RINL, Hindustan Shipyard, HPCL, IT parks, Eastern Naval Command.
Post offices, March 2016: keyed Anantapuramu (G2 Mains 2017); the app's earlier notes said Chittoor – not verified. Latest: Prakasam (post offices); Visakhapatnam (bank branches, mobile connections).
2025-26 GVA (current prices): services 43%, agriculture 33%, industry 24%; manufacturing 10.84%.
2024-25 FRE: GSDP ₹15.91 / ₹8.67 lakh cr (current / constant); largest current GVA = Services ₹6.11 lakh cr; AP 8th by GSDP.
CAG: fiscal deficit ₹31,717 crore = 6.10% of GSDP in 2014-15 – slightly more than double the FRBM ceiling of 3%.
Exam angle: CAG figures – RD ₹13,776 cr, FD 6.10% (≈ double the 3% ceiling); gap grant ₹3,979.50 cr; appointed day 2 June 2014.
CAG monthly accounts: RD ₹54,355 crore by Nov 2025; CAG flagged a high revenue deficit three years running.
CAG on power subsidy: spending at 121% (2023) and 120% (2024) of budget estimates.
Off-budget borrowings (CAG): ₹1,18,394 crore (Mar 2022) → ₹1.28 lakh crore = 9.7% of GSDP (Mar 2023).

Interest = charged item (not voted); fixed, non-developmental; more than doubled since 2017-18. Sustainability signs: debt-GSDP and interest/revenue receipts; golden rule – borrow only for capital assets. AP runs a primary deficit → borrowing also funds current spending.

Off-budget = loans by State PSUs/corporations repaid from the State budget, outside reported debt, used to get around FRBM caps; ₹1.28 lakh cr, 9.7% of GSDP (Mar 2023, CAG 2024); ₹1,40,470 cr (31 Mar 2024).
2014-15 debt-GSDP (first year after bifurcation): sources differ – a CAG table ~28.2%, a Lok Sabha reply 23.9%; the APPSC options (28.19–29.63%) remain unsettled.
Grants-in-aid share: 23.6% of revenue receipts in 2016-17; 15% in 2024-25 BE. CAG 2015-16: own tax ≈ 45%.
CAG: only ₹1.05 lakh cr (48% of estimate) collected by Nov 2025; non-tax under one-fifth of BE.
Section 47(4): disputes settled by Central order on the advice of the CAG (the CAG only advises).
Irrigation component at 2013-14 prices ₹20,398.61 crore; balance as on 1.4.2014 ₹15,667.90 crore (Finance Ministry note).
CAG (audit to Mar 2023): settle submergence issues with neighbours with PPA; build protective embankments (due by 2014-15).
AP, Bihar and Odisha still demand SCS (as of January 2026).
Polavaram: Centre funds 100% of the remaining cost of the irrigation component (cost as on 1 April 2014).

Financial division: Part VI, "Apportionment of Assets and Liabilities", Sections 47-67 (the money items are Sections 47-64, Sec 64 = residuary; 76-83 = services); disputes settled by mutual agreement, failing which by Central order on the advice of the CAG (Sec 47(4)).
CAG (2019): ₹1,51,349.67 crore under capital heads and ₹28,099.68 crore of loans and advances still not apportioned between AP and Telangana (still pending after 7 years).
Undivided AP (NARP): 7 zones (incl. North and Southern Telangana; Krishna-Godavari as one zone).
Operational SEZs in AP: 19 (2016-19 figure, as of January 2019; also the APPSC G2 answer to "how many SEZs") – now 25 operational, 30 notified (Lok Sabha reply, 30 Nov 2023).
Simhadri (NTPC, Visakhapatnam): 2,000 MW (as of April 2025).

UN Secretary-General presents an annual SDG Progress Report (global indicator framework); the Global Sustainable Development Report is produced every four years for the quadrennial review – not every quarter.

Expansions: 2024 – ASHA, Anganwadi workers and helpers and families; Ayushman Vay Vandana card (Oct 2024) – Rs 5 lakh for all aged 70+ regardless of income. Odisha and Delhi latest to join (April 2025).
new: Expansions: 2024 – ASHA, Anganwadi workers and helpers and families; Ayushman Vay Vandana card (Oct 2024) – Rs 5 lakh for all aged 70+ regardless of income. Odisha and Delhi joined in April 2025; **West Bengal** is the latest to join (MoU with NHA, 8 June 2026) – the **36th State/UT**, so PM-JAY now runs in all States/UTs.
why: West Bengal signed the PM-JAY MoU on 8 June 2026, becoming the 36th State/UT; Odisha and Delhi are no longer the latest

text: Most moons: Saturn – 274 after 128 were confirmed (March 2025); March 2026: the Minor Planet Center added 15 (11 Saturn, 4 Jupiter) → Saturn 285, Jupiter 101 (as of 2026).
new: Most moons: Saturn – 274 after 128 were confirmed (March 2025); 2026 additions by the Minor Planet Center (11 in March, 7 in April, 1 in June) → **Saturn 293**, **Jupiter 115** (as of June 2026).
why: Further moons announced in April and June 2026 raised Saturn to 293 and Jupiter to 115 (NASA APOD, Aug 2026)

text: Coriolis force = an apparent force caused by the Earth's rotation (not revolution, tilt, pressure, temperature or magnetism); it shapes winds, ocean currents, cyclones and large-scale weather patterns.

Cause: electric currents in the liquid outer core – convection of molten iron = geodynamo (UPPCS 2011) – not a giant magnet at the centre. It shields life from solar wind and cosmic radiation; flow changes are linked to reversals.

North magnetic pole: first located (1831) on the Boothia Peninsula, northern Canada – UPSC 2005 key; it has since drifted into the Arctic Ocean towards Siberia (~86°N as of 2025, World Magnetic Model 2025).
Order: 1912 Wegener → 1930s Arthur Holmes (convection currents; heat from radioactive decay) → 1960–62 Hess (sea-floor spreading) → 1963 Vine–Matthews → 1967 plate tectonics.

FAO Status of the World's Soil Resources 2026 (3 Sep 2026): threats led by soil erosion; soil biodiversity loss ranked 4th of seven, after erosion, loss of soil organic carbon and nutrient mismanagement.
Conditions for a delta: heavy sediment load, slow flow, shallow sea, weak tides and currents (strong tides remove sediment).
Main agent of coastal erosion: waves (also tides, currents, tsunamis, humans). Processes: hydraulic action, abrasion, attrition, solution (saltation is wind).
APPSC G2 2024 match: Delta – running water; Cirque – glaciers; Cliffs – waves and currents; Sand dunes – winds (a-III, b-IV, c-I, d-II).
Most hot deserts lie between 15° and 30° N and S, on the western margins of continents (subtropical highs, offshore trade winds, cold currents).
Bougainville: autonomous region of Papua New Guinea; voted ~98% for independence (Nov–Dec 2019, non-binding); PNG parliament still to ratify (as of 2026; target 2027–30).
Wind on a hot summer day = convection current of air (CDS 2011); trade winds too arise from convection (Hadley cell).
Heat surplus in the tropics, deficit at the poles; winds and ocean currents carry heat poleward.
Controls: latitude, altitude (Himalayas cool), distance from sea, ocean currents (cold currents lower coastal temperature), relief, cloud cover.
None in the South Atlantic and SE Pacific – UPSC 2015 key: ITCZ seldom occurs there; also cold currents (Benguela, Humboldt) keep SST low.

Hot deserts 15–30°, on western margins; most likely near 23° (Tropics): subtropical high pressure + offshore trade winds + cold currents. Sahara, Kalahari, Namib, Atacama, Arabian, Thar, Great Australian.

El Nino = an abnormally warm ocean current that appears off the coast of Peru and Ecuador in the eastern (and central) tropical Pacific and flows south along the west coast of South America, replacing the cold Peruvian (Humboldt) current. It is an ocean event, not an air mass, a wind or a low-pressure centre (CDS 2011).
The El Nino current carries warmer, less saline water (the warm, rain-freshened pool of the western Pacific spreads east) – NDA 2010 "all four" statements.
APPSC: Peru warm current + "Christ child" + 2014 Indian rainfall deficit = all three correct.

Warm currents flow from the equator towards the poles, usually on the east coasts of continents in low and middle latitudes; cold currents flow towards the equator, usually on the west coasts (NCERT).

Odd ones: Humboldt is NOT warm (APPSC); Agulhas is NOT cold; Kuroshio is NOT cold; Canary is NOT warm and not in the Pacific; Benguela does not flow in the North Atlantic; Peruvian is the only Pacific current among Benguela, Brazil, South Equatorial.
Pairs of warm currents: North Atlantic Drift and Brazil; all cold: Humboldt and Benguela; Canaries and Benguela.
Tidal currents: tidal water channelled between islands or into bays and estuaries forms tidal currents.
Best fishing grounds form where warm and cold ocean currents meet (mixing brings nutrients and plankton), mainly between 40° and 60° – asked 4 times (APPSC 2002 twice, UPSC 2013 twice).
The Labrador Current meets the Gulf Stream at the Grand Banks, not near Vancouver Island (NDA 2010: I and II only).
Cold currents on west coasts help form arid climates; warm currents warm the coasts beside them; currents keep Earth's heat balance.

Ocean currents = large masses of surface water circulating in regular patterns; the slow surface movement of water, set in motion mainly by prevailing winds, help keep the heat balance, are affected by the configuration of the ocean – UPSC 2002: all four statements correct.
Equatorial Counter Current flows west to east between the North and South Equatorial Currents (through the doldrums) because their convergence piles up water in the west (UPSC 2015, asked twice).
Surface currents = upper 400 m, about 10% of ocean water; deep currents = 90%.

Waves = oscillations moving energy; tides = periodic vertical rise and fall; currents = continuous horizontal flow with major effects on climate, fisheries and navigation; currents redistribute heat, so they influence climate.

Sargasso Sea (North Atlantic): the only sea with no coastline – bounded by currents: Gulf Stream (W), North Atlantic Drift (N), Canary (E), North Equatorial (S); calm, warm, salty; named after its floating Sargassum weed (typical marine vegetation).
